characterList.description: A male doctor with short brown hair and blue eyes. He wears blue and green scrubs and a backpack in some scenes.
characterList.name: Dr. Cellini

content_metadata.description: This video offers a concise and practical guide to reading a chest X-ray, focusing on a systematic approach and highlighting key features. The opening scene engages the viewer with its energetic style, while the main content provides clear and informative instructions. The final scene encourages viewers to engage with Dr. Cellini on social media.

qAndA.answer: He starts by looking at the lung apices to rule out a pneumothorax.
qAndA.question: Where does Dr. Cellini begin his analysis of the chest X-ray?

qAndA.answer: He has seen many missed fractures on chest X-rays and wants to ensure he doesn't miss any.
qAndA.question: Why does Dr. Cellini check the bones on the chest X-ray even though it's not a bone X-ray?

qAndA.answer: He refers to adjusting the brightness and contrast of the image to better visualize specific structures.
qAndA.question: What does Dr. Cellini mean by 'windowing' the X-ray image?

qAndA.answer: He uses it to pinpoint the location of abnormalities seen on the frontal view and to look for pleural effusions in the costophrenic angles.
qAndA.question: How does Dr. Cellini use the lateral view of the chest X-ray?

qAndA.answer: He checks for free air, which would appear as a dark crescent shape.
qAndA.question: What does Dr. Cellini look for under the diaphragm on the lateral view?
